options.name: Institute a Vacancy Freeze
options.who_is_affected: City workforce; freezing non-critical vacant positions (10-20% deemed critical) avoids personnel costs. Bears on departments needing to fill roles.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($143.7M) assumes 20% of vacancies critical; high end ($161.7M) assumes 10% critical. One-time savings for FY2026.
options.dissent_summary: Two dissents (p16). Dissent A argues it goes TOO FAR: freezing hiring overlooks long-term consequences—overtime, burnout, heavier reliance on contractors. Dissent B argues it DOES NOT GO FAR ENOUGH: should eliminate CPD officer vacancies older than two years (1,126 CPD vacancies), shift parking enforcement to Dept of Finance, and route mental-health/social calls to the CARE team.
options.verbatim_anchor: freezing hiring for non-critical vacant positions

options.name: Continue Overtime Reduction
options.who_is_affected: City departments (CPD, CFD, Water Mgmt, Aviation, Streets & Sanitation) through better staff-resource management, not service reduction.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($52.1M) assumes 15% reduction in overtime; high end ($69.5M) assumes 20%; based on FY2024 actuals. Timing of Savings stated as One-Time.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p17-18) argues it DOES NOT GO FAR ENOUGH: should eliminate CPD overtime, which exceeded budget by >2x recently ($170M over in 2024, $224M in 2023, $138M in 2022). CPD should cap overtime so no officer spends more than 5% over allocated overtime.
options.verbatim_anchor: further reducing annual overall overtime by 15-20%

options.name: Streamline Hiring
options.who_is_affected: City and labor unions; accelerating hiring of revenue-generating roles (legal, parking enforcement) under Shakman decree constraints.
options.feasibility_note: Operates under court-mandated Shakman decrees; $25M is incremental annual revenue from accelerated hiring of revenue-generating roles.
options.verbatim_anchor: pursuing any and all efficiencies in its hiring process

options.name: Implement Flexible Furlough Days
options.who_is_affected: Union and non-union City employees, who take scheduled unpaid leave; requires negotiation with labor unions.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($9.4M) assumes one furlough day for union and non-union in FY2026; high end ($18.8M) assumes two. One non-union day = $0.7M; one union day = $8.7M.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p19) argues it goes TOO FAR / is counterproductive: furloughs damage morale, raise turnover and recruitment/training costs, and can trigger overtime that offsets savings; City should pursue workforce stability instead.
options.verbatim_anchor: enacting 1-2 flexible furlough days

options.name: Improve Succession Planning
options.who_is_affected: City departments (CDPH, DFSS, DPD) with high retirement-eligible staff; centralizing succession planning in HR.
options.feasibility_note: Not possible to estimate financial results; expected to create efficiencies over time.
options.verbatim_anchor: centralizing succession planning and knowledge transfer efforts within HR

options.name: Explore Cost Savings from Potential Employee Contribution Opportunities
options.who_is_affected: City employees through changes to contributions, salary caps, or surcharges; requires labor-union negotiation.
options.feasibility_note: Illinois Constitution Art. XIII Sec. 5 limits pension-contribution changes to new hires; Social Security safe-harbor compliance required. $41.6-52.2M annual.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p21) argues it goes TOO FAR: increasing healthcare costs via premium/coverage changes degrades the benefits package and hurts recruitment/retention; City should pursue real cost-control reforms instead of shifting costs.
options.verbatim_anchor: exploring cost saving opportunities associated with various employee contributions

options.name: Identify Cost-Saving Options Where CBA Talks are Unnecessary
options.who_is_affected: Non-union employees (contribution adjustments), former employees (COBRA), HMO stop-loss; no CBA negotiation required.
options.feasibility_note: Includes eliminating HMO stop-loss, claims/fee integrity study, COBRA communications, workers-comp return-to-work program. $17.3-25.3M annual.
options.verbatim_anchor: cost saving opportunities where negotiation is not required within a CBA

options.name: Explore Healthcare Plan Design Opportunities
options.who_is_affected: City employees via plan options, copay/out-of-pocket alignment to peer median; requires labor-union negotiation.
options.feasibility_note: $12M annual; aligning plan design closer to Chicago's peer jurisdiction median.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p22) argues it goes TOO FAR: increasing employee healthcare costs through premium/coverage changes degrades the benefits package and harms recruitment/retention; City should pursue real cost-control reforms.
options.verbatim_anchor: cost saving opportunities within healthcare plan design

options.name: Explore Network/Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBM) and Carrier Cost Saving Opportunities
options.who_is_affected: City employees via narrowed carrier networks, expanded Centers of Excellence, refined PBM contracts; requires LMCC cooperation.
options.feasibility_note: $10.1-13.5M annual; requires cooperation with the Labor Management Cooperative Committee (LMCC).
options.verbatim_anchor: cost saving opportunities related to network/PBM and carrier networks

options.name: Assess Cost Savings from Health Coverage Continuation on Extended Leave of Absence (LOA)
options.who_is_affected: Employees on extended LOA; some pay contributions, others none, with cost borne by the City. Requires labor-union negotiation.
options.feasibility_note: Estimated savings not available; only where benefits are not mandated.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p23) argues it goes TOO FAR: most employee groups already pay 100% of health insurance on LOA after FMLA is exhausted; most extended leaves are health-related, so modifying policy to further hinder healthcare access is wrong. City should instead enhance SSDI/Medicare application assistance.
options.verbatim_anchor: assessing health coverage continuation for employees on extended LOA

options.name: Implement CFD Fire Alarm Inspection, Hazmat Material Fee, High-Rise Fire Fees
options.who_is_affected: Parties receiving CFD fire alarm inspections, hazmat responses, and high-rise fire responses; new fees introduced.
options.feasibility_note: $6.2M in year 1, $68.3M over ten years. Fees at peer max: fire alarm inspection $498, hazmat response $1,800, high-rise fire $540.
options.verbatim_anchor: recovering costs incurred by CFD for fire alarm inspection

options.name: Disband CPD Mounted Unit Division
options.who_is_affected: CPD mounted unit (25 horses, 17 officers, 4 sergeants, 1 lieutenant); personnel reassigned to vacant patrol positions.
options.feasibility_note: $5.9M net FY2026 savings: $5.8M from reassigning personnel plus a one-time $0.1M from sale of all 25 horses.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p26) argues it goes TOO FAR: mounted horses remain an effective crowd-control tool and play an important ceremonial role.
options.verbatim_anchor: disbanding CPD's mounted units division

options.name: Implement CFD False Fire Alarm Fee Cost Recovery
options.who_is_affected: Commercial and personal properties causing false fire alarms; new escalating fee.
options.feasibility_note: $6.6M year 1, $72M over ten years. Low end ($4.7M) assumes first false-alarm fee waived; high end ($6.6M) assumes not waived. Fees escalate $500/$667/$833/$1,000.
options.verbatim_anchor: recovering the cost of CFD responding to false fire alarms

options.name: Implement CPD False Burglar Alarm Cost Recovery
options.who_is_affected: Parties causing false burglar alarms requiring CPD response; new escalating fee ($0/$0/$115/$215).
options.feasibility_note: $2.8M year 1; assumes false-alarm instances decrease after fee introduced.
options.verbatim_anchor: recovering the cost of CPD services responding to false burglar alarms

options.name: Divert CFD 911 Calls to Hospital-Based Telehealth Service
options.who_is_affected: Non-emergency 911 callers redirected to hospital telehealth triage; reduces ambulance dispatch volume. Requires labor-union cooperation.
options.feasibility_note: $2.2M personnel efficiencies + $0.5M from 6-7 fewer ambulances, net of $0.2M upfront training = $2.5M net year 1.
options.verbatim_anchor: reducing unnecessary ambulance dispatches by partnering with hospitals

options.name: Improve CFD Cost Recovery of Pyrotechnics, Sprinkler Plan Review
options.who_is_affected: Parties requiring pyrotechnics permits and sprinkler plan review; existing fees raised to peer levels.
options.feasibility_note: $1.6M in FY2026. Fees: pyrotechnics $600/permit; sprinkler plan review $731 first 100 + $5/head + $200 resubmittal.
options.verbatim_anchor: increasing cost recovery for CFD pyrotechnics and sprinkler plan review

options.name: Increase CPD First Time Driving Under the Influence (DUI) Fee
options.who_is_affected: First-time DUI offenders; fee raised from $500-$2,500 to peer max $5,000 (Seattle, Philadelphia).
options.feasibility_note: $1.1-1.3M annual ($1.1M year 1). Repeat-offense fees could raise more.
options.verbatim_anchor: increasing its fee for a first DUI offense to match its peer maximum

options.name: Institute CFD Emergency Medical Service (EMS) Cost Recover - Treat-No-Transport (TNT)
options.who_is_affected: People treated on-scene without transport; Medicare/Medicaid (~70% of TNTs) exempt. Flat fee up to $1,050.
options.feasibility_note: $0.9M year 1 at $1,050 TNT peer max (NYC); peers bill $150-$1,050.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p29) argues it goes TOO FAR: charging a ~$1,000 fee to 911 callers not transported yields under $1M but could harm the underinsured and deter people from calling for help when needed.
options.verbatim_anchor: instituting a treat-no-transport (TNT) fee

options.name: Increase Use of Autonomous Drones at CPD
options.who_is_affected: CPD aerial operations; replaces one Bell 206 helicopter with six autonomous drones. Subject to Illinois surveillance law.
options.feasibility_note: $0.4M net year 1 ($0.5M savings less $0.1M one-time drone investment). Illinois law prohibits general public surveillance.
options.dissent_summary: Two dissents (p30). Dissent A argues it goes TOO FAR: expanded drone surveillance/data collection raises tracking concerns and may erode residents' sense of security. Dissent B argues it is INADEQUATE: the drones are not sufficient to replace a helicopter and may not meet CPD's needs.
options.verbatim_anchor: replacing one Bell 206 helicopter unit with six autonomous aerial drones

options.name: Institute CFD Cost Recovery for Non-Emergency Lift Assist
options.who_is_affected: Assisted living facilities / nursing homes (not the individual) for non-emergency lift assists; $550 per lift (peer max, Bangor ME).
options.feasibility_note: $0.3M in FY2026. Charged to the facility, not the individual. Phased approach would reduce savings.
options.verbatim_anchor: fee to recover costs incurred by CFD for Non-Emergency Lift Assistance

options.name: Increase CPD Cost Recovery for Squad Car Usage in Film Production
options.who_is_affected: Film productions using CPD squad cars; fee raised from $150 to $200 per car per day (peer max, Columbus).
options.feasibility_note: $0.2M annual; recovers wear and tear on cars.
options.verbatim_anchor: increasing the amount of cost recovery incurred by squad car usage in film production

options.name: Maximize CPD Civilianization
options.who_is_affected: Sworn officers in administrative roles, replaced by civilian personnel so officers resume frontline duties.
options.feasibility_note: Savings not available; recommend waiting to develop strategy until the ongoing CPD staffing study is released.
options.verbatim_anchor: maximizing the use of civilian employees in CPD administrative positions

options.name: Rent OPSA Regional Training Facility
options.who_is_affected: External public-safety agencies renting the Public Safety Training Center (PSTC) during non-use; community concerns about PSTC.
options.feasibility_note: Year-1 net impact is -$0.2M (upfront cost); grows to $0.5M incremental revenue by FY2027. Negative figure is the Year-One investment.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p32) argues it goes TOO FAR / objectionable: CPD's documented history of misconduct and consistent community opposition to the PSTC; any leasing must comply with the Welcoming City Ordinance and not compromise public confidence.
options.verbatim_anchor: renting facility space and equipment to external public safety agencies at PSTC

options.name: Expand OPSA Utilization of Cameras in CFD Vehicles and Utilize Existing CPD Cameras
options.who_is_affected: CFD vehicle fleet (~250 units) outfitted with cameras to reduce accidents/abuse; aims to cut accident-related repair costs.
options.feasibility_note: Year-1 net -$0.5M (upfront $2,000/camera install); generates $1.3M net recovery FY2027, rising to $3.4M by FY2030. Assumes 70% drop in accident repair costs (per Baltimore).
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p33) argues it goes TOO FAR: cameras are a punitive approach that fosters distrust and harms recruitment/retention; prefer enhanced driver training and smart traffic-control technologies.
options.verbatim_anchor: utilizing existing CPD cameras and adding cameras where absent in CFD vehicles

options.name: Introduce CFD Light-Duty Positions
options.who_is_affected: CFD personnel on lay-ups (injury leave) transitioned to light duty to shorten recovery; reduces lay-up overtime.
options.feasibility_note: Year-1 net -$0.7M (clinician/benefit investment); must be bargained per CBA, so savings begin FY2027 (~$5.7M net). Assumes 20% overtime savings on lay-ups ($36M lay-up overtime in 2024).
options.verbatim_anchor: introducing light-duty positions in CFD that will expedite returns from lay-ups

options.name: Implement a CPD Early Warning System (EWS)
options.who_is_affected: CPD officers flagged for risk patterns; aims to reduce settlements/judgments (averaged $43M/yr over four years).
options.feasibility_note: Year-1 net -$1.5M (two-vendor cost, consent-decree mandated); grows to $5.2M by FY2030, $1.2M FY2027, if per-officer settlement cost falls to peer average (11% reduction).
options.verbatim_anchor: implementing an EWS to flag officers who exhibit patterns of behavior

options.name: Reclaim Costs for Non-City-Sponsored Parades
options.who_is_affected: Organizers of private (non-City-sponsored) parades; ordinance amended for full cost recovery. Excludes City-sponsored parades.
options.feasibility_note: $11.9M annual; requires amending ordinances. Excludes City-sponsored parades (Memorial Day, Halloween).
options.verbatim_anchor: amending ordinances to allow for full cost recovery for private parades

options.name: Maximize CPD Cost Recovery for Events
options.who_is_affected: Private festivals, athletic events, stadium events; recovers CPD non-overtime costs (currently only overtime reimbursed).
options.feasibility_note: $5.5M annual incremental cost recovery of non-overtime CPD costs.
options.verbatim_anchor: maximization of recoverable CPD non-overtime costs

options.name: Reclaim Other Personnel Costs to Improve Special Event Cost Recovery
options.who_is_affected: Festival and stadium event organizers; recovers CFD/CDOT/DSS personnel costs via ordinance amendment.
options.feasibility_note: $1.5M annual; requires amending ordinances to allow recovery of CFD/DSS/CDOT personnel costs.
options.verbatim_anchor: amending ordinances to allow recovery of personnel costs from CFD, DSS and CDOT

options.name: Reclaim Non-Personnel Costs to Improve Special Event Cost Recovery
options.who_is_affected: Festival and stadium event organizers; recovers non-personnel costs (barriers, medical equipment, protective gear) via ordinance amendment.
options.feasibility_note: $1.3M annual; currently non-personnel recovery allowed at athletic events only.
options.verbatim_anchor: additional cost recovery for non-personnel expenditures at festival and stadium events

options.name: Capture Non-Personnel Costs for Athletic Events to Improve Cost Recovery
options.who_is_affected: Private athletic event organizers; applies existing 'commissioner's discretion' non-personnel recovery more consistently.
options.feasibility_note: $0.6M annual based solely on non-CPD personnel overtime.
options.verbatim_anchor: recovering other allowable non-CPD personnel and non-personnel costs for private athletic events

options.name: Utilize Full Overtime Rate to Improve Cost Recovery
options.who_is_affected: Private special-event organizers (outside stadium events); recovers full 1.5x overtime rate vs. current 1.4x.
options.feasibility_note: $0.2M annual. NOTE: a section-level dissent (p39) appears immediately after this option — see dissent_summary; its attachment is ambiguous between this option and the broader Special Events cost-recovery approach.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p39) offers an ALTERNATIVE: because smaller private events cannot afford policing costs, provide free services from CARE Team members and Violence Interrupters rather than police at events. (Placement is ambiguous; reads as a section-level dissent on charging private events for policing.)
options.verbatim_anchor: applying and recovering the full allowable rate (1.5x regular hourly rates)

options.name: Improve Data Tracking and Collection
options.who_is_affected: City departments tracking special-event costs; auto-generated event ID codes enable cost capture from event organizers.
options.feasibility_note: No direct dollar estimate; expected multiplier effect on other special-event cost-recovery savings.
options.verbatim_anchor: improving the consistency and structure of data collection across departments

options.name: Optimize Maintenance and Repair Unit (MRU)
options.who_is_affected: City fleet (15,000+ assets, 36 departments) and MRU labor force; multi-shift/seasonal flex labor. Requires labor-union negotiation.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($5.1M) assumes 5% savings in repair/maintenance spend; high end ($10.2M) assumes 10%. Savings ramp in later years.
options.verbatim_anchor: enhancing labor efficiency used to repair and maintain the fleet

options.name: Accelerate Disposition Process
options.who_is_affected: City's surplus/long-term-hold vehicles managed by 2FM; decommissioning, possibly via third-party brokers.
options.feasibility_note: Low end assumes ~2,600 vehicles at ~$1,800/vehicle; high end reflects higher resale via third-party brokers. One-time revenue, but annual gains possible.
options.verbatim_anchor: effectively disposing of vehicles managed by 2FM that have reached end of useful life

options.name: Establish Fleet Utilization Metrics
options.who_is_affected: City fleet operations; utilization targets, KPIs, vehicle pooling, right-sizing.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($2.9M) assumes 2% savings on addressable spend; high end ($5.8M) assumes 4% plus ~5 added vehicle coordinators.
options.verbatim_anchor: developing and maintaining utilization targets, tracking metrics, and KPIs

options.name: Improve Lifecycle Modelling / Replacement Strategy
options.who_is_affected: City fleet procurement; data-driven vehicle replacement timing via Optimum Vehicle Replacement Lifecycle (OVRC).
options.feasibility_note: $2.2-4.4M annual; based on OVRC informing optimal replacement timing to minimize total ownership cost.
options.verbatim_anchor: improving vehicle procurement policies by incorporating a new data-driven approach

options.name: Expand Warranty Recovery
options.who_is_affected: City fleet maintenance; maximizing use of contractually obligated warranty coverage. Needs ~2 added FTEs.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($1.7M) assumes 2% savings on parts and labor spend; high end ($3.7M) assumes 4%.
options.verbatim_anchor: enhancing vehicle warranty management to maximize utilization of available coverage

options.name: Improve Procurement Process
options.who_is_affected: City vehicle procurement; standardizing exception management in purchasing.
options.feasibility_note: $0.2-0.4M annual; standardized exception management process for fleet purchasing.
options.verbatim_anchor: improving upon existing controls and allowances for exceptions during vehicle procurement

options.name: Extend Advanced Pension Policy Beyond 2028
options.who_is_affected: City's four pension funds; advance payments above statutory minimum reduce future liability and contribution needs.
options.feasibility_note: Estimated savings 'Not available' in table; if policy extended through 2055 it forecasts ~$2.6 billion in savings (per Center for Tax and Budget Accountability).
options.verbatim_anchor: extending its Advanced Pension Policy beyond its current expiration date of 2028

options.name: Consider Feasibility of Instruments Available to Reduce Pension Costs and Liabilities
options.who_is_affected: City's four pension systems (combined funded ratio 26.2% in FY2024); Pension Obligation Bonds (POB), pension buyouts.
options.feasibility_note: Savings not available; recommends actuarial analyses (made public) before pursuing any specific proposal.
options.verbatim_anchor: studying the feasibility of re-amortizing and reducing pension debt

options.name: Shift Timing of Pension Contributions
options.who_is_affected: City's pension funds; contributing at the start of the fiscal year for more compounding time.
options.feasibility_note: Savings not available; notes there is always risk of a negative market return.
options.verbatim_anchor: shifting the timing of its pension contributions to the beginning of the fiscal year

options.name: Modernize Technology Systems
options.who_is_affected: City-wide IT platforms; eliminating duplicative software, updating legacy systems, strengthening cybersecurity.
options.feasibility_note: Savings not available; high-level only — more detailed IT analysis in the final report. Six themes outlined (ops, redundant spend, data governance, security, AI/responsiveness, training).
options.verbatim_anchor: a system-wide modernization of its technology platforms

options.name: Implement Category Management (CM) System
options.who_is_affected: City procurement (~$4.6B/year, ~27% of budget); reduces duplicative procurement, optimizes vendor relationships.
options.feasibility_note: Body states CM could save an estimated $55-$111M once fully implemented over a 3-5 year period; the Efficiencies summary table lists Procurement as N/A (not counted in near-term totals).
options.verbatim_anchor: implementing CM to reduce duplicative procurement efforts across departments

options.name: Improve Financial Deposit Management
options.who_is_affected: City Treasurer / City deposit accounts; transferring funds to higher-yield accounts to capture interest income.
options.feasibility_note: Savings not available; recommends a regular review cadence and custodian-update steps.
options.verbatim_anchor: systematically monitor its financial deposit accounts

options.name: Expand Congestion Surcharge (Rideshare)
options.who_is_affected: Rideshare/TNP riders (excluding taxis); surcharge extended to congested census tracts, airports, Navy Pier, McCormick Place.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($26M) extends to eight additional congested tracts (~25% of congestion); high end ($103M) assumes citywide extension.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p69) argues it goes TOO FAR / is misguided: the tax lacks clarity of purpose (congestion vs. environment vs. revenue), exempts taxis/commercial/private vehicles, and adds access fees that discourage downtown visits when occupancy is already low; City should focus on revitalizing transit and downtown.
options.verbatim_anchor: extending the Congestion Surcharge imposed on transportation network providers

options.name: Increase Garbage Fee to Improve Cost Recovery
options.who_is_affected: Households paying the monthly garbage fee (currently $9.50; seniors 50% off); DSS true cost ~$320M vs ~$60M collected.
options.feasibility_note: Three approaches: Option A phased to $12.50 (~$20M, FY2026); Option B immediate $55 to cover total DSS costs (~$296.9M); Option C immediate $37 for direct costs (~$179.5M). All keep 50% senior discount.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p72) argues it goes TOO FAR / is regressive: lower-income homeowners already struggle with rising costs; City should seek progressive revenue from wealthy residents and corporations and offer garbage collection without a fee, like New York.
options.verbatim_anchor: increasing the garbage collection fee to cover a more substantial portion

options.name: Revisit Retail Delivery Fees
options.who_is_affected: Recipients of food/package deliveries by traditional delivery operators; requires State legislation.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($6.1M) assumes $0.10/delivery; high end ($30.4M) assumes $0.50/delivery; 53 deliveries/household/year. Jurisdiction: State.
options.verbatim_anchor: revisit State legislation that would allow the City to implement fees for deliveries

options.name: Consider Advertising on Light Poles
options.who_is_affected: Advertisers paying a monthly streetlight-banner program fee; new revenue stream on City light-pole infrastructure.
options.feasibility_note: $4.3M based on 1% of City light poles carrying two banners each.
options.verbatim_anchor: a new revenue stream through a streetlight banner advertising program

options.name: Adjust Fees for Sidewalk Café Permit
options.who_is_affected: Sidewalk café permit holders; tiered rates unchanged since 2000 raised for inflation and tied to property values.
options.feasibility_note: $3.1M year 1; proposed rates $25/$12/$5 per sq ft by demand zone; rates adjusted biennially by Chicago MSA CPI after a real estate assessment.
options.verbatim_anchor: adjusting the current sidewalk café permit fee of $600

options.name: Adjust Certification of Zoning Compliance Fee
options.who_is_affected: Applicants for zoning-compliance certification; fee ($120, set 2007) below peer average ($180).
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($1M) raises fee to $179 by cumulative inflation; high end ($2.6M) raises to peer max $282 (Dallas).
options.verbatim_anchor: adjusting certification of zoning compliance fees

options.name: Adjust Limited Business License Fees
options.who_is_affected: Limited business license holders; fee ($250, set 2012) below peer average ($373).
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($0.9M) raises fee to $340 by cumulative inflation; high end ($3.1M) raises to peer max $568 (Minneapolis).
options.verbatim_anchor: adjusting limited business license fees

options.name: Adjust Driveway Permit Fee
options.who_is_affected: Driveway permit applicants; fee ($120, unchanged since 2015) below peer average ($265).
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($0.8M) raises fee to $158 (inflation since 2015); high end ($9.3M) raises to peer max $560 (Cincinnati).
options.verbatim_anchor: adjusting the driveway permit fee to account for inflation since 2015

options.name: Explore a Road Usage Charge
options.who_is_affected: Road users; potential Motor Fuel Tax replacement as vehicles shift to fuel-efficient/electric. Requires State dialogue.
options.feasibility_note: $0.6M; recommends beginning a dialogue with the State. Jurisdiction: State.
options.verbatim_anchor: beginning a dialogue with the State to assess a Road Usage Charge

options.name: Develop an Intellectual Property (IP) Licensing Program
options.who_is_affected: Third parties licensing City trademarks (municipal 'Y', CPD/CFD logos, 'Chicago'/'Windy City'); new non-tax revenue.
options.feasibility_note: ~$0.6M net year 1; net of licensing agent fees and two FTEs for enforcement.
options.verbatim_anchor: developing a formal IP licensing policy to generate non-tax revenue

options.name: Adjust Canopy Permit Fees
options.who_is_affected: Canopy permit applicants; fee ($855, set 2019) below peer average ($1,255).
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($0.5M) raises fee to $1,057 (inflation since 2019); high end ($1.8M) raises to peer max $1,666 (San Diego).
options.verbatim_anchor: adjusting canopy permit fees to account for cumulative inflation since 2019

options.name: Adjust Zoning Permit Review Fees for Renovations and Alterations
options.who_is_affected: Applicants for renovation/alteration zoning permit review; fee ($75, set 2013) below peer average ($159).
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($0.5M) raises fee to $101 (inflation); high end ($4.2M) raises to peer max $300 (Charlotte).
options.verbatim_anchor: adjusting zoning permit review fees for renovations and alterations

options.name: Adjust Fees for Food Violation Citations
options.who_is_affected: Establishments cited for food violations; fee ($500, set 2018) raised for inflation/peers.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($0.4M) raises to peer average $572; high end ($1.8M) raises to peer max $1,000 (Washington DC). Inflation-only would be $631.
options.verbatim_anchor: adjusting food violation citation fees to account for cumulative inflation

options.name: Adjust Annual Food Inspection Fees
options.who_is_affected: Food establishments; annual inspection fees ($100-$550, set 2005) raised by square footage.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($0.3M) inflation-adjusts to $157-$864; high end ($0.8M) raises to peer max $616 (Dallas).
options.verbatim_anchor: adjusting the City's annual food inspection fees

options.name: Adjust Zoning Permit Review Fees (New Construction)
options.who_is_affected: New-construction zoning permit applicants; fee ($75, set 2013) below peer average ($261).
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($0.2M) raises fee to $101 (inflation); high end ($2.7M) raises to peer max $419 (Charlotte).
options.verbatim_anchor: adjusting zoning permit review fees for new construction

options.name: Expanding Digital Outdoor Advertising
options.who_is_affected: Private media company partner; City receives 40% of revenue from digital signage along Riverwalk/high-traffic areas.
options.feasibility_note: Program could generate ~$1-1.3M total; City share ~$0.2-0.3M (40% revenue-share). Media company gets 60%.
options.verbatim_anchor: expanding its digital advertising program to include public infrastructure

options.name: Adjust Barricade Permit
options.who_is_affected: Barricade permit applicants; fee ($550, set 2019) raised for inflation/peers.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($0.1M) raises to $683 (inflation since 2019); high end ($3.3M) raises to peer max $1,078 (Philadelphia).
options.verbatim_anchor: adjusting barricade permit fees to account for cumulative inflation since 2019

options.name: Adjust Dumpster Permit Fees
options.who_is_affected: Dumpster permit applicants; fee ($290) raised for inflation/peers.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($0.1M) raises to peer average $334 (also cited as $341 by inflation); high end ($1.8M) raises to peer max $500 (Milwaukee).
options.verbatim_anchor: adjusting dumpster permit fees to account for cumulative inflation

options.name: Adjust Parking Vehicle Fees
options.who_is_affected: Parties parking vehicles/equipment on public right-of-way (CDOT-administered); fee below peer average ($68).
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($0.1M) inflation-adjusts; high end ($0.8M) raises to peer max $120 (Miami).
options.verbatim_anchor: adjusting parking vehicle fees administered by CDOT

options.name: Adjust Sign Permit Fees
options.who_is_affected: Sign permit applicants; fees ($200-$500, set 2007) raised for inflation/peers.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($0.1M) raises to peer max $281 (Dallas); high end ($0.3M) inflation-adjusts $586 to $748.
options.verbatim_anchor: adjusting the City's sign permit fees to account for cumulative inflation

options.name: Index Fees and Fines to Inflation Annually
options.who_is_affected: Payers of value/unit-based fees and fines; CPI-indexed annually (not percentage-based fees/fines).
options.feasibility_note: Estimated revenue N/A; applied to extent increases align with peer jurisdictions.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p79) argues it goes TOO FAR for certain regressive charges: towing, vehicle immobilization, storage, and city sticker fees should NOT be auto-CPI-adjusted, as they disproportionately harm lower-income households and can lead to job loss and debt.
options.verbatim_anchor: indexing all value or unit-based fees and fines to the CPI

options.name: Adjust Code Enforcement Fines
options.who_is_affected: Parties cited for code violations; current fines $500-$10,000+ raised toward peer levels.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($0.6M) raises to peer average $2,189; high end ($1.4M) raises to peer max $2,717 (Seattle).
options.verbatim_anchor: adjusting code enforcement fines to its peer average of $2,189

options.name: Adjust Recycling Fines
options.who_is_affected: Parties cited for recycling violations; fines ($300-$1,000, set 2000) raised for inflation/peers.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($0.5M) raises to peer average $1,081; high end ($2.1M) raises to peer max $2,500 (New York). Inflation would raise first violation to $1,139.
options.verbatim_anchor: adjusting recycling fines to account for cumulative inflation

options.name: Maintain Grocery Tax
options.who_is_affected: Grocery shoppers (SNAP exempt); City must pass a local ordinance by Oct 1, 2025 to continue the 1% grocery tax.
options.feasibility_note: $80M (2% inflation estimate on $77M 2024 collections) to $83M (alternative approach). State sets Oct 1, 2025 deadline.
options.verbatim_anchor: maintaining the 1% grocery tax previously levied and distributed by the State

options.name: Expand Sales Tax on Services
options.who_is_affected: Consumers of services (salons, tattoo parlors, warehousing/storage, insurance, etc.); requires State action.
options.feasibility_note: $78-305M range reflects conservative-to-optimistic modeling; assumes State expansion generates $2B, of which $78M to the City. Jurisdiction: State.
options.verbatim_anchor: requesting State lawmakers expand the sales tax to broadly encompass all consumer services

options.name: Adjust Liquor Tax
options.who_is_affected: Liquor purchasers; shift from unit-based (unchanged since 2008) to percentage-of-value tax.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($60M) assumes 3% value-based tax; high end ($120M) assumes 6%; both assume unchanged consumption.
options.verbatim_anchor: adjusting its Liquor Tax from a unit-based tax to a percentage of value-based tax

options.name: Adjust the City's Property Tax
options.who_is_affected: Property owners; resume annual CPI levy adjustment (suspended 2023), with a possible homeowner rebate/relief program.
options.feasibility_note: $56M if CPI increase resumed in 2026. Recommends a rebate to exempt certain homeowners for equity.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p55) argues it goes TOO FAR / should not be automated: Chicago already imposes among the highest commercial property taxes; rising property taxes have discouraged investment, raised office vacancy, and shifted burden to neighborhoods. Over-reliance on property taxes is a structural problem to be solved, not automated; City should pursue pro-growth policies.
options.verbatim_anchor: resuming annual adjustments to its Property Tax levy by CPI in 2026

options.name: Increase Share of Local Government Distributive Fund (LGDF)
options.who_is_affected: City (via State income-tax distribution); requesting State revert to 2011 share (10%); requires State action.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($35M) assumes a 0.5% share increase; high end ($250M) assumes returning to a 10% share. Jurisdiction: State.
options.verbatim_anchor: requesting the State revert to the 2011 percentage share of state income tax

options.name: Update Amusement Tax (Resellers)
options.who_is_affected: Online-only ticket resale companies and registered brokers; requires State to update 'broker' definition.
options.feasibility_note: $35-38M; assumes full 9% amusement tax applied to markups/fees of online resale companies, or State 'broker' redefinition with 3% applied to total resale price. Jurisdiction: State.
options.verbatim_anchor: requesting the State update its definition of ticket broker

options.name: Apply 911 Surcharge to Digital Prepaid Wireless Services
options.who_is_affected: Users of digital 'prepaid' wireless plans (true prepaid calling cards remain at lower rates); requires State action to close loophole.
options.feasibility_note: $12.5M/year to the Corporate Fund plus $27.5M/year to the Emergency Communication Fund. Jurisdiction: State.
options.verbatim_anchor: close a loophole in monthly wireless plan charges for digital prepaid services

options.name: Adjust Bottled Water Tax
options.who_is_affected: Bottled water purchasers; rate ($0.05/bottle, unchanged since 2008) increased.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($8.4M) is a $0.03 increase to $0.08/bottle (inflation 2008-2025); high end ($27.9M) is a $0.10 increase to $0.15/bottle.
options.verbatim_anchor: increasing the current bottled water tax rate of $0.05 per bottle

options.name: Increase Plastic Checkout Bag Tax
options.who_is_affected: Shoppers using plastic checkout bags; tax raised from $0.10 to $0.15; retailers currently keep $0.01 of $0.10.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($2.3M) sunsets retailer share and keeps full $0.10; high end ($13M) raises tax to $0.15 and removes retailer share. Peer: Philadelphia.
options.verbatim_anchor: increasing the plastic checkout bag tax from $0.10 to $0.15

options.name: Reinstitute the Head Tax
options.who_is_affected: Employers with >50 employees (previous $4/employee tax repealed 2013, raised ~$20M from 2,000+ taxpayers).
options.feasibility_note: $10.2-25.6M; urge City first study whether repeal increased business registrations before reinstating.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p59) argues it goes TOO FAR: head taxes disincentivize hiring, especially for medium-sized businesses, encourage avoidance/relocation, and discourage office tenancy amid record vacancy. Cites Amazon pausing HQ over Seattle's head tax; City should pursue pro-growth policies.
options.verbatim_anchor: reinstituting an employer's head tax

options.name: Initiate Internet Gaming Tax
options.who_is_affected: Online sports bettors (98% of betting is online, currently untaxed); $0.25-$0.50 tax per online wager.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($8.5M) assumes $0.25/wager; high end ($17M) assumes $0.50/wager; both assume ≥20% of State bets placed in City and 10% loss to avoidance.
options.verbatim_anchor: placing a $0.50 tax on all wagers placed via online betting

options.name: Pursue Payments in Lieu of Taxes (PILOT) Program
options.who_is_affected: Tax-exempt institutions (medical, educational, cultural) making voluntary payments to offset tax exemptions.
options.feasibility_note: Low end ($0) assumes no voluntary payments; high end ($52M): medical $30.4M (4), educational $20.2M (4), cultural $1.6M (1). Peers: Boston, Baltimore, Providence.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p60) argues it goes TOO FAR / is improper: all 50 states exempt nonprofits from property tax; PILOTs circumvent existing law, violate the spirit of the nonprofit exemption, and the ad-hoc, non-transparent negotiation is often viewed as coercive rather than truly voluntary.
options.verbatim_anchor: pursuing a PILOT program to collect voluntary payments from tax-exempt institutions

options.name: Optimize the City's Real Estate Portfolio
options.who_is_affected: City real estate (500+ buildings, 10,400 vacant land parcels) via consolidation, disposition, lease renegotiation.
options.feasibility_note: $29.5M revenue in Year 1. Asset monetization category; includes some recurring lease elements but reported as a Year-1 figure.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p61) argues partially TOO FAR: selling vacant office buildings brings one-time income but loses future revenue potential; better to give those assets time to be reactivated. No objection to selling vacant lots.
options.verbatim_anchor: optimizing its real estate portfolio through strategic consolidation, disposition

options.name: Declare Maximum TIF Surplus
options.who_is_affected: TIF districts; surplus declared as one-time measure (FY2025 surplus was $570M). Tiered sweep of active districts.
options.feasibility_note: $137M based on FY2025-size surplus and state-law distribution; some TIF surplus already in FY2026 forecast. Acknowledged as unpredictable one-time revenue.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p62) argues it goes TOO FAR / is short-sighted: TIF funds were created for capital projects/infrastructure (CTA, schools, parks, libraries); diverting surplus undermines them, and using TIF surplus as a recurring fix encourages dependence on unstable one-time revenue.
options.verbatim_anchor: declaring the maximum TIF surplus as a one-time measure

options.name: Favor Allowing Natural Expiration of TIFs
options.who_is_affected: TIF districts set to expire (13 expiring 2026, 9 candidates for extension); returns EAV to City tax base.
options.feasibility_note: $11M in additional property tax revenue ($1.5M from four already flagged + $9.5M from nine flagged for extension). Recommends transparent TIF-efficacy metrics.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p63) opposes prioritizing expiration: City must already secure General Assembly approval for extensions (existing scrutiny); rather than favoring expiration, the City should work collaboratively with local alders/legislators to fast-track important infrastructure (schools, parks, CTA, libraries) instead of stalling them on rigid metrics.
options.verbatim_anchor: revising its TIF extension policy to favor allowing more TIFs to naturally expire

options.name: Explore Early Termination of TIFs
options.who_is_affected: Select TIF districts nearing expiration; early closure returns property value to tax base sooner.
options.feasibility_note: Estimated revenue not available; described as complex (legal/financial requirements, early bond retirement).
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p63) argues it goes TOO FAR: terminating TIFs early provides short-term revenue but undermines TIFs' long-term purpose and risks scuttling community investment and capital projects that schools, parks, and neighborhoods rely on.
options.verbatim_anchor: exploring the feasibility of early termination for select TIF districts

options.name: Clarify and Document CPS MEABF Pension Payments
options.who_is_affected: City and CPS; the $175M pension payment to MEABF on behalf of CPS, not yet reimbursed, adds to City's unfunded liability.
options.feasibility_note: Estimated revenue not available. City, CPS, and State should agree on which entity assumes the MEABF payment going forward.
options.verbatim_anchor: the City and CPS should reach an agreement on which entity will be assuming the MEABF pension payment

options.name: Shift to Outcome-Based Budgeting
options.who_is_affected: City budgeting process; ties expenditures to measurable results vs. prior-year spending.
options.feasibility_note: Future cost savings not estimable; helps prevent fiscal leakages and improve allocation.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p65) argues it goes TOO FAR without guardrails: tying funding to outcome measures can set unrealistic standards and reduce access to services for those with the most barriers; a purely outcomes-based program without significant guardrails is opposed.
options.verbatim_anchor: pursuing a shift from traditional budgeting to an outcome-based budgeting approach

options.name: Establish Autonomous Taxi Framework
options.who_is_affected: Future autonomous taxi operators; permitting framework generates non-tax revenue, may cannibalize ground-transport tax.
options.feasibility_note: $34.5-36.3M Year 1 if autonomous taxis begin operating. Low/high ends reflect aggressive vs. conservative estimates of cannibalized ground-transport tax. Jurisdiction: City/State.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p66) is a caution (not strictly for/against): extreme care should be taken so the permitting framework does not drastically stifle innovation or investment in the Chicago market, which is tied to positive resident experience.
options.verbatim_anchor: establishing a permitting framework for autonomous taxis

options.name: Establish Autonomous Water Taxis and Freight Framework
options.who_is_affected: Future autonomous water-taxi operators; licensing/docking/advertising fees offset displaced charter vessel revenue.
options.feasibility_note: $0.89M net Year 1. Assumes 12 autonomous water taxis by year 1, 24 by year 10; $10,000/year vessel license, $5,000/year docking. Requires alignment with US Coast Guard and IL DNR. Jurisdiction: City/State/Federal.
options.verbatim_anchor: establishing a permitting framework for autonomous water taxis and freight vessels

options.name: Establish Autonomous Freight Drone Framework
options.who_is_affected: Future autonomous freight-drone operators; permitting/licensing/advertising for federally regulated drone operations.
options.feasibility_note: Header lists revenue as 'Not available'; body cites 10-year revenue $0.10-$0.29M and Year 1 $0.01M (annual payments) to $0.03M (upfront lump sum at 50% discount). FAA is federal regulator. Jurisdiction: City/Federal.
options.dissent_summary: Dissent (p67) is a caution (not strictly for/against): extreme care should be taken so the permitting framework does not drastically stifle innovation or investment in the Chicago market, which is tied to positive resident experience.
options.verbatim_anchor: creating a permitting framework for autonomous freight drones

notes: TOTALS: 89 options (Efficiencies 45, Revenues 39, Other 5), matching the report's Executive Summary (p7). Aggregate fiscal impact stated as $1,037.8M low to $2,145.4M high (p7); Efficiencies $372.4-455.5M; Revenues $630.0-1,652.7M; Other $35.4-37.2M. AMBIGUITIES/CAVEATS: (1) Special Events dissent on p39 (free CARE/Violence Interrupter services for small private events instead of police) is placed between 'Utilize Full Overtime Rate' and 'Improve Data Tracking'; it reads as a section-level dissent and its precise option attachment is ambiguous — attached here to 'Utilize Full Overtime Rate'. (2) Several Public Safety options carry NEGATIVE Year-1 dollar figures (Rent OPSA Training -$0.2M; Cameras in CFD Vehicles -$0.5M; CFD Light-Duty -$0.7M; EWS -$1.5M); per the report's footnote (p24) these are upfront Year-One investments that turn positive over a 10-year horizon — captured as stated negatives. (3) Implement Category Management (Procurement): body gives $55-111M long-term estimate but the Efficiencies summary table lists Procurement as N/A; captured the body figure with a feasibility caveat so it isn't double-counted in near-term totals. (4) Extend Advanced Pension Policy: table N/A, but body forecasts ~$2.6 billion savings if extended through 2055 (one-time/long-horizon, not annual) — left dollar_estimate null and noted. (5) Autonomous Freight Drone: revenue header says 'Not available'/table N/A, but body cites $0.10-0.29M (10-yr) and $0.01-0.03M (Year 1) — left null, body figures in feasibility_note. (6) Garbage Fee high end ($296.9M) is the most aggressive of three options (A/B/C); range captured as $19.6M (Option A phased) to $296.9M (Option B immediate). (7) Several revenue options are State-jurisdiction (Sales Tax expansion, LGDF, Amusement Tax resellers, 911 surcharge, Retail Delivery Fees, Road Usage Charge) requiring State action — noted in feasibility. (8) 25 of 89 options carry a formal dissent.
